Map your engineering skills before you open a role

How HR and technical leaders can map the skills in their engineering teams before hiring, and decide what to hire for, train for or secure.

  1. Home
  2. Insights
  3. Map your engineering skills before you open a role

24 November 2026 · 4 min read

  • Article
  • HR leaders
  • Technical leaders

Most hiring requests start with the most urgent problem: a project is late, someone has resigned, a customer wants a new capability. The request becomes a job title, the job title becomes an advert, and nobody stops to ask whether the skill is already in the company, or whether hiring is the best way to get it.

A competence map answers that question before you spend months on a search. This article explains what one contains, how to build it and how to turn it into decisions.

Job titles hide competences

Two engineers with the same title can have very different skills. One “senior automation engineer” may be an expert in safety systems, another in robot programming. A “DevOps engineer” may know your cloud platform deeply, or mainly your build pipelines.

Headcount by role tells you how many people you have. It doesn’t tell you what they can do, how deep that knowledge goes, or what happens if one of them leaves. That is the information you need to decide whether to hire.

What a competence map contains

A useful competence map has four parts:

  1. A competence framework for each discipline in scope: the skills that matter for your work, written in your teams’ language. For a software team, that might include system design, testing, cloud infrastructure and security practices. For a plant engineering team, PLC programming, functional safety, maintenance planning and process improvement.
  2. Level descriptions for each competence, described as what someone can do: from “works on it with guidance” to “designs it, and teaches others”.
  3. A skills matrix: people or roles against competences, with their assessed level.
  4. A gap analysis: where the levels fall short of what your plans require, and where knowledge sits with only one person.

How to build one in practice

Start small. One team, one site or one critical discipline is enough to learn how the method works in your company. You can extend it later with the same framework.

Define the competences with your technical leads. HR can run the process, but the competences must come from the people who do the work. Keep the framework short enough to assess: a long list of narrow skills turns into a form nobody completes properly.

Combine several sources. A self-assessment for each person, a review by their manager, and structured interviews with people in key roles, run by someone who knows the discipline. Self-assessments alone are unreliable: some people underrate themselves, others overrate. Together, the sources give a picture you can trust.

Agree up front how the data is used. Tell people why you are mapping competences, who sees individual results and how long they are kept, in line with GDPR. A map built on trust gives better data than one people fear.

Reading the results: hire, train or secure

The map is useful because it separates problems that look the same from the outside. For each gap, ask:

  • Is the skill missing, but learnable by people you already have? Train for it. A targeted training plan costs less than a hire and keeps your best people growing.
  • Is it missing, rare and needed now? Hire for it, with a role profile built from the map rather than a generic job title.
  • Is it there, but held by only one person? That is a single point of failure. Plan knowledge transfer and a successor before that person moves on.
  • Is it needed only for one project or a temporary peak? An independent specialist engaged for the project may be the better answer.

You will usually find all four. That is the point: one hiring request often hides a training need and a continuity risk.

Common pitfalls

  • Turning it into a performance review. The aim is to map the skills of teams and roles, not to rate individuals. If people think the map decides their bonus, they will tell you what you want to hear.
  • Listing tools instead of competences. Tools change; the competence behind them lasts longer. “Version control” is a competence; a specific product is evidence of it.
  • Measuring everything. Focus on the competences that drive your plans for the next two or three years.
  • Doing it once. A map is a snapshot. Revisit it when strategy, technology or the team changes, using the same framework so the results are comparable.

From map to hiring brief

When the map shows that a role must be hired, it also gives you most of the brief: the competences that are missing, the level required and the context the person will work in. That makes the search faster and the technical interview sharper, because everyone knows exactly what to test.

Our competence mapping service delivers a skills matrix, a gap analysis and a recommendations report, built with engineers who know the discipline. From there, talent acquisition fills the gaps to hire for, and succession planning addresses the single points of failure.
